summary:
Same-sex relations are legal throughout Italy for men and women, and the age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation, a parity Italy has held since before the twentieth century. Cross-dressing is legal; the fascist penal code of the 1920s–1940s banned it and police targeted transgender people during that period, and a police officer was reportedly dismissed in 2006 for cross-dressing in public while off duty.

Italy has no single comprehensive statute covering sexual orientation and gender identity; protection rests on court rulings and sectoral laws. Sexual-orientation discrimination in employment has been illegal nationwide since July 2003 under Legislative Decree no. 216 of 2003, implementing EU Directive 2000/78/EC, with the exemptions for police, armed forces and rescue services removed by Law no. 101 of 2008. No nationwide law explicitly bans transphobic discrimination, so transgender people may face discrimination in goods and services, housing, education and health care; ILGA-Europe's 2021 report noted the absence of nationwide protection for goods and services. A Rome court ruled on 15 January 2023 that firing a trans professor amounted to sex discrimination.

Legal gender change has been possible since 1982, when Italy became the sixth country worldwide to allow it; since 21 May 2015 neither sterilisation nor sex reassignment surgery has been required. On 23 July 2024 the Constitutional Court, in judgment no. 143, first recognised non-binary individuals as rights-holders under Articles 2, 3 and 32 but declined to add a non-binary registry marker, holding that only Parliament can alter the male/female binary, and struck down the requirement of judicial authorisation for gender-affirming surgery after a legal sex change. Courts in Trento (15 February 2023) permitted legal gender change for transgender minors with parental consent and psychological consultation, and Trapani (6 July 2023) allowed a name and gender change with no surgery or hormones.

On 14 April 2025 the Supreme Court of Cassation ordered Italian identity cards to use the gender-neutral term "genitori" rather than "mother" and "father" for children with same-sex parents, finding the previous wording discriminatory. Citing the Constitutional Court's 2010 ruling recognising same-sex couples as a "legitimate social formation," the Court of Cassation ordered a questura to grant a residence permit to an Algerian citizen married to a same-sex Spanish spouse. Italy recognises persecution based on sexual orientation or gender identity as grounds for asylum under the 1951 Geneva Convention and EU Qualification Directive 2011/95/EU, and Decree-Law No. 130/2020, in force 22 October 2020, simplified asylum procedures and reinforced protection for vulnerable groups including those persecuted on those grounds. Same-sex marriages performed abroad are registered as civil unions rather than marriages (Court of Cassation, May 2018).

Since February 2019 puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones have been provided free of charge under the National Health Service, and since 2020 hormone therapy has been fully covered. In 2018 the Italian National Bioethics Committee and the Italian Medicines Agency backed puberty blockers for adolescents with gender dysphoria case by case with safeguards; access requires medical evaluation, parental consent and exhaustion of other interventions, a position supported by the Italian Society of Endocrinology, the Italian Academy of Pediatrics and six other paediatric and medical societies. Gay and bisexual men have been allowed to donate blood since 2001.

On 7 April 2026 ANSA reported that convictions were upheld on appeal for the assault of transgender tourists in Italy, a court outcome affirming accountability for violence against trans visitors. On 5 July 2024 tgcom24 reported that a Milan traffic officer was sentenced to 10 months for beating a transgender woman with a baton. The ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering 2025) records that the Education Ministry omitted LGBTI persecution from Holocaust Remembrance Day circulars for a second year, that a cardinal called homosexual acts "a mortal sin," that homophobic and transphobic violence continued including organised dating-app entrapment schemes targeting gay men, and that in March the Civil Court of Asti recognised for the first time physical and psychological harm from homophobic mistreatment. HRW's World Report 2025 Italy chapter records political rhetoric hostile to LGBT people contributing to a hostile environment, alongside constraints on the rule of law and civil society.

A bill banning homophobic and transphobic advertising in streets and on vehicles passed the Chamber of Deputies 271–16 on 28 October 2021 and the Senate 190–34 on 4 November, was signed by President Mattarella and took effect 10 November 2021; the government forced a single up-or-down vote on the whole bill, so MPs who opposed that provision had to vote for it. A broader anti-discrimination and hate-crime bill passed the Chamber 265–193 on 4 November 2020 but died in the Senate on 27 October 2021 by a 131–154 secret ballot. Regional anti-discrimination statutes cover Tuscany (2004), Liguria (2009), Marche (2010), Sicily (2015), Piedmont (2016), Umbria (2017), Emilia-Romagna (2019), Campania (2020) and Apulia (2024).

In May 2026 AGESCI, Italy's largest Catholic scout association, decided that sexual orientation and gender identity can no longer exclude adults from leadership and educational roles, after three years of internal debate. Pew found in 2013 that 86% of Italians aged 18–29 accepted homosexuality, against 67% of those over 50.
tangentialFactors:
Progetto Gionata reports that transphobia is the most atroce and diffuse discrimination facing transgender people in Italy, an advocacy characterisation rather than a measured prevalence figure. Intrepid Travel presents Italy as an LGBTQIA+ destination for its travellers; the page carries no safety finding specific to Italy.

The Pew acceptance figures date from 2013 and measure attitudes toward homosexuality, not gender identity, and are more than a decade old; they should be read as historical context rather than current opinion.
localsOnly:
A Ludwig Boltzmann Institute national report of July 2025 examines LGBTIQ detainees in Italy, covering homolesbobitransphobia and discrimination, pathways to gender affirmation, same-sex relationships, and the legal and policy framework for LGBTIQ people in Italian detention. A 2026 thematic analysis in Frontiers in Psychiatry examines transgender identity and psychiatric care in Italian prisons, identifying systemic gaps and institutional challenges for incarcerated trans people.

Regional anti-discrimination statutes, distinct from the national employment protections, are in force in Tuscany (2004), Liguria (2009), Marche (2010), Sicily (2015), Piedmont (2016), Umbria (2017), Emilia-Romagna (2019), Campania (2020) and Apulia (2024), so residents' protection against discrimination outside employment varies by region of residence.
outOfScopeNotes:
The ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 entry for Italy and the HRW World Report 2025 chapter are cited here through secondary description; the underlying PDFs were not read in full for this pass, so any additional trans-specific findings in those documents remain unresolved.

The ANSA report of 7 April 2026 on the appeal convictions for the assault of transgender tourists does not specify the date of the underlying assault, the sentence imposed, or the jurisdiction within Italy; those details are not sourced here.

The tgcom24 report of 5 July 2024 on the Milan officer's 10-month sentence does not state whether the sentence was upheld on appeal or served; later procedural history is unresolved.

No current (post-2021) national survey measuring Italian attitudes specifically toward transgender people, as distinct from homosexuality, appears in this inventory; the 2013 Pew figures are the most recent attitudinal data available here and concern homosexuality only.
